title: Poland to Hold Rates as Fuel-Price Cap Seen Cooling Inflation
paragraphs: Poland’s central bank is set to keep interest rates on hold for a seventh straight month as the government’s move to reduce fuel prices at the pump buys policymakers more time to assess inflation path.

The Monetary Policy Council will hold its benchmark at 3.75% on Wednesday, according to all 34 economists surveyed by Bloomberg. The panel is expected to announce its decision before 4 p.m. in Warsaw, while Governor Adam Glapinski is scheduled to hold his monthly news conference at 3 p.m. on Thursday.

The MPC’s decision comes after the government revived measures to shield customers from spiking fuel prices. The move is set to slow inflation to 3.3% in October from a 15-month peak of 4% set in September, according to economists at Credit Agricole Bank Polska SA.
“Despite the sharp rise in inflation in September, the governor will temper market expectations regarding interest rate hikes,” the lender’s chief economist Jakub Borowski said.

Nevertheless, he expects a rate hike in November to anchor inflation expectations and limit second-round risks of high fuel costs. The 10-member MPC targets price growth over the medium-term at 2.5%, with a tolerance band of plus/minus one percentage point.

Traders have pared wagers on Polish rate hikes as the government introduced caps on fuel prices starting last Saturday, according to forward-rate agreement contracts. Still, a quarter point in monetary tightening remains likely in either November or December, said Wood Finance Ltd.’s chief economist Raffaella Tenconi.

Glapinski — who last month said that rates could stay on hold until mid-2027 — sounded more hawkish in comments made on Sept. 30, just days before the new fuel measures were announced. The central bank “will act responsibly and decisively to keep inflation low,” the governor said.

title: HSBC Executive Strikes Back in Court Fight Over Poaching Claims
paragraphs: An HSBC Holdings Plc executive who’s spent years fighting allegations by First Citizens Bank & Trust Co. that he raided staff and stole trade secrets is now seeking to turn the tables, saying his accuser broke the law.

HSBC and executive David Sabow have fiercely contested a $1 billion lawsuit alleging he spearheaded an illicit scheme to hire more than 40 people from his past employer, Silicon Valley Bank, after its 2023 collapse and subsequent acquisition by First Citizens’ parent company. In a recently filed counter-attack, Sabow claims First Citizens is trying to enforce a non-compete agreement that violates California law by interfering with the freedom of workers to change jobs.

“Rather than compete fairly for talent and clients, after Mr. Sabow turned down First Citizens’ offer to lead its own innovation banking business, First Citizens sued him for offering a lifeline to his former colleagues,” his lawyers wrote in a court filing.
Late last week, a US magistrate judge said he can pursue his counterclaim, rejecting a request from First Citizens to rule that he filed it too late.
Talent poaching can be particularly bitter for banks because client relationships are among their most valuable assets, directly tied to deposits and loans at the heart of their core business.
The high-stakes dispute playing out in San Francisco federal court offers a window into how messy it can become for everyone involved when companies sue over employee defections.
Three years after First Citizens went to court, the Raleigh, North Carolina-based company has seen most of its claims thrown out and now must engage its lawyers to play defense.

“There’s nothing wrong with coworkers banding together to go somewhere else,” said Orly Lobel, a law professor and founding director of the Center for Employment and Labor Policy at the University of San Diego.
First Citizens and HSBC both declined to comment.

The downfall of SVB in 2023 amid a regional banking crisis opened up a rare chance for its competitors to step into venture banking. At its peak, SVB boasted that it banked nearly half of all venture capital-backed technology and life sciences companies in the US.

When it collapsed, bankers scrambled for new jobs, taking with them the relationships that make up the innovation economy. They landed at places including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and Stifel Financial Corp., which each saw an opportunity to win over SVB’s coveted clients by mirroring its business model.

First Citizens initially won big by bringing over thousands of SVB bankers through the 2023 acquisition, which catapulted the family-controlled firm into the ranks of the 15 largest US banks by assets.
But Sabow, who had spent a decade at SVB and headed its tech and healthcare banking in North America, went to HSBC, one of the largest banks in Europe, along with many members of his team.
Based in California, SVB was a relatively easy target for a talent lift. The Golden State has long barred most non-compete agreements.
Sabow’s new counterclaim hinges on those very protections. He argues that the employment agreement he was required to sign in 2012 to join SVB cannot now be enforced against him by First Citizens.

“Through its lawsuit, First Citizens seeks to accomplish what California law expressly forbids: restraining employee mobility through an unlawful post-employment noncompetition agreement,” lawyers representing Sabow and HSBC said in a July filing.
First Citizens shot back in late August, arguing in a filing that Sabow waited too long to file his counterclaim and it should be dismissed as “both unauthorized and untimely.”
But in an Oct. 1 ruling, US Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler said Sabow’s motion was “properly asserted” — which means he can pursue it against First Citizens.

In its initial complaint in May 2023, First Citizens portrayed the mass defection of 42 employees on the morning of Easter Sunday as an elaborate scheme by HSBC to plunder the “core of SVB’s profitability engine.”

The suit identified Sabow as the “chief architect” of the raid — which was code-named “Project Colony” — and accused him of building his plan around a proprietary SVB memo detailing the bank’s employees and clients, including how much profit it made from each borrower.

HSBC countered that it “lawfully extended job offers” to workers whose employment status was up in the air after SVB’s collapse. Sabow denied that the written memo included any proprietary information, and said he hired the bankers in question to help them rebuild their careers.

In 2024, Beeler threw out many of First Citizens’ claims, saying the allegations “show only a failed bank and employees decamping to a better business opportunity.” In May, Beeler declined to revive the dismissed claims.
But Sabow, who was promoted by London-based HSBC last year to be its head of global innovation banking, isn’t out of jeopardy himself. He still faces breach of contract and trade-secret theft claims.

First Citizens’ hunt for evidence that Sabow failed to honor his contractual obligations to SVB continues. Court filings indicate that after obtaining some 66,000 pages of documents and more than 1,000 mobile communications, his accuser has gained some traction.

In August, Beeler said First Citizens can search the personal devices of one of Sabow’s fellow defectors after it was revealed that he had emailed a spreadsheet of SVB client information from his personal account to his HSBC account.

She also ordered documents to be turned over by two other former SVB employees, one of whom photographed confidential information on his computer screen and emailed the photos to himself — a method that Beeler noted leaves “no forensic trail.” HSBC has argued there was no wrongdoing in the conduct identified by the magistrate.

HSBC has stood by Sabow since his hiring. His promotion last year put him in charge of the global expansion of the company’s venture-banking business, which provides deposit accounts, loans and other services to startups and VC funds.

At the pace the case has progressed, it could still be a year or more before it goes to trial — if it doesn’t settle first, or after all the evidence is submitted, Beeler doesn’t dismiss it entirely. However the fight ends, it won’t be the last time the banking talent wars end up in court.

In early September, Citizens Financial Group, a Providence, Rhode-Island based lender with $234 billion in assets, accused rival SoFi Bank of poaching more than 30 mortgage department employees across six states, and that the loss of Citizen Financial staff in Connecticut “essentially eliminated its market presence.”
Salt Lake City-based SoFi said in a statement: “This is a baseless allegation and a clever attempt to prevent Citizens employees from pursuing career opportunities elsewhere.”
The case is First-Citizens Bank and Trust Company v. HSBC Holdings Plc, 23-cv-02483, US District Court, Northern District of California (San Francisco).

title: The Reclusive Houthi Leader Wreaking Havoc in the Middle East
paragraphs: Abdul Malik al-Houthi had never met an international diplomat before. Clothed in traditional Yemeni dress, he waited patiently at a modest house in the country’s isolated north, his hair apparently freshly cut.

It was April 2011, and Yemen was on the brink of all-out civil war with anti-government protests, part of the wave of regional uprisings known as the Arab Spring that was spreading across the Middle East. The United Nations envoy to the country at the time, Jamal Benomar, eventually arrived to meet the little-known commander of the Houthis, dismissed by many as a ragtag militia.

“The guy you meet is a gentleman, speaks with a soft voice, extremely polite,” recalled Benomar, who said he was the only diplomat known to have met al-Houthi in person. “Even if he doesn’t like what you are saying, he will never interrupt and stop you from saying something he doesn’t like.”
Fifteen years later, that reserved 31-year-old has become one of the Middle East’s most consequential and enigmatic figures.

Al-Houthi presides over a militant group that’s taken over swathes of Yemen, often brutally suppressing the people under its control. The Houthis’ reach extends far beyond the country as they disrupt global trade, rattle energy markets and fire missiles at Saudi Arabia, whose allied forces on the ground are leading a coalition that vowed at the weekend to eliminate them.

Proscribed as a terrorist organization by Donald Trump’s administration, the Houthis amassed an arsenal capable of reaching hundreds of miles, striking oil facilities and commercial shipping in the Red Sea. They launched deadly drone attacks at Israel. In September, they seized control of territory overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.

They also raised their ranking within Iran’s so-called Axis of Resistance. As Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon were battered in the conflicts that followed the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks on Israel, the Houthis grew more confident about their own value to the alliance.

They are taking on some of the role that Hezbollah played under Hassan Nasrallah, who was killed by an Israeli strike two years ago, said Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group and author of a book on the Axis of Resistance. “Not simply as another member of the network, but as a hub connecting and supporting other actors,” he said.

The Houthis ousted Yemen’s government in 2014, imposing a repressive rule, recruiting child soldiers and embroiling Yemen in a civil war. It provoked one of the worst humanitarian crises in a nation that was already one of the poorest in the world.

Yemen’s internationally recognized government last weekend launched a full-scale military campaign to retake territory after weeks of escalating clashes between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia dragged Yemen back into a fully-fledged conflict.

But after surviving more than two decades of war, the Houthis are more emboldened than ever before. Their leader inherited the group as a young man when it was fighting for survival in Yemen’s remote, mountainous north. They now rule the capital, Sanaa, and most of Yemen’s north and western coastline, home to roughly 70% of the population.

Al-Houthi’s rise is all the more striking given how little of the world he had seen. There is no evidence he ever travelled to Iran or even saw much of Yemen. Al-Houthi rarely meets outsiders. He holds no formal position in the Houthi administration and is seldom seen beyond televised speeches delivered from an undisclosed location, emulating the late Hezbollah leader Nasrallah. Few know where he lives.
Born in 1979 in Saada, an impoverished province bordering Saudi Arabia, al-Houthi grew up in one of northern Yemen’s prominent families of Zaydi religious scholars.

His father, Badr al-Din al-Houthi, was a prominent cleric who spent much of his life teaching and writing about the Zaydi faith, a branch of Shia Islam distinct from the Twelver Shiism dominant in Iran.

Badr al-Din had four wives and a large family. His eldest son, Hussein, became a politician and charismatic preacher whose teachings laid the ideological foundations of the Houthis, according to Marieke Brandt, author of Tribes and Politics in Yemen: A History of the Houthi Conflict and a senior researcher at the Austrian Academy of Sciences.

“Hussein was such an influential figure that his impact was felt across the family and his generation,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Houthi official who has long worked with al-Houthi, said over Telegram. “He played a major role in shaping Abdul Malik’s thinking and his views on many issues and events.”

Al-Houthi had little formal education beyond his family’s religious world, according to Maysaa Shuja al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, who has followed the Houthi movement closely for many years. He never acquired the scholarly credentials of his father or older brother, instead making his name on the battlefield because of his military capabilities, she said.

Yemeni forces killed Hussein al-Houthi in September 2004, at the end of the first of six wars with Saleh’s government in Saada. The movement then gradually coalesced around his younger brother, who was earning a reputation as a commander of guerilla forces.
What made him stand out was “his ability to deal with difficult circumstances, earn the trust of those around him, and demonstrate his leadership in practice,” said al-Bukhaiti.
The government repeatedly tried and failed to crush the Houthis in their northern stronghold during the Saada wars. They survived, but the areas around them in Saada were devasted by years of war.

“The shelling was so intense that he could no longer tell from the sound when his rifle magazine was empty,” said al-Bukhaiti. “He only realized when the rifle stopped recoiling against his shoulder.”

The Saada wars forged the circle that remains closest to al-Houthi. Many of the senior figures around him today are men who fought alongside him during those years and power remains concentrated at the top.

The Houthis leave little room for those who stray from their political, social or religious line. Successive crackdowns have swept up critics and people working for foreign aid organizations. Women face restrictions on their movement, work and public life, while religious minorities have been subjected to persistent discrimination and persecution.

The renewed fighting has also taken a heavy toll. At least 838 people have been killed and more than 3,600 injured in Yemen since the Houthis resumed hostilities with the internationally recognized government in August, according to the World Health Organization. Many Yemenis have fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti.

Al-Houthi once regularly met with a wide range of Yemenis, but as his power has grown, so too has his isolation. Shuja al-Deen said al-Houthi is “paranoid” and doesn’t trust people easily. Al-Bukhaiti said his seclusion is a security necessity after repeated attempts to kill him, while Al-Houthi keeps a tight grip on the decisions that matter most.

“He rarely gives direct orders, preferring to explain what he wants and bring others with him,” said al-Bukhaiti. When the two first worked together, his instructions were so understated that al-Bukhaiti said he sometimes mistook them for advice.

Ali al-Bukhaiti, a former Houthi official and Mohammed’s brother, remembers al-Houthi in 2011 as shy and attentive, often sitting silently through meetings and listening closely. “Personally, I still love him to this day,” said Ali, who later broke with the Houthis. “But I disagree with his ideas.”

As he urged the international community to take the Houthis seriously that year, Benomar said he set out to bring Yemen’s powerbrokers together for dialogue before it was too late. He wanted everyone with influence in the country to be involved, including the young leader of the Houthis.

Tahrir Square in central Sanaa was filled with young people demanding change and an end to President Ali Abdullah Saleh’s three-decade rule. Saleh’s government was jostling with opponents over the country’s future. Few were paying much attention to the rebel movement from the north.

After coordinating with Mahdi al-Mashat, then in his mid 20s and now president of the Supreme Political Council of the Houthis, Benomar traveled north to Saada. He left his UN security detail behind and passed through a series of Houthi checkpoints to reach the stronghold. Benomar remembers driving through rubble and ruins, entire areas levelled by years of fighting.
But the group al-Houthi runs today was galvanized by that destruction.

The Houthis are routinely described as an Iranian proxy. But al-Houthi’s relationship with Tehran developed gradually, initially through the group’s ties with Hezbollah. The Houthi takeover of Sanaa in 2014 forced Tehran to take the group more seriously. After the Saudi-led coalition started attacking Yemen a year later, the Houthis were driven closer to Iran.

Hezbollah was the model. The Lebanese group had survived wars with a far more powerful military power, Israel, while building military and political power. The Houthis sought to replicate that in Yemen. Iran saw that as an opportunity to widen its Axis of Resistance. The Houthis then increasingly became beneficiaries of Iranian expertise, weapons and training.
“They don’t need to be a proxy if they have the same agenda and the same goals,” Shuja al-Deen said. “Iran doesn’t need to give them orders.”

Ties between the Houthis and Tehran entered a new phase after Israel launched its war on Gaza in 2023 in response to Hamas swarming into the south of the country, massacring 1,200 people and taking another 250 hostage. The Houthis began firing missiles and drones toward Israel and targeting commercial shipping in the Red Sea, saying they were acting in support of Palestinians.

The campaign boosted al-Houthi’s regional and international profile and cemented the Houthis as a force to be reckoned with. The US has kept intact the truce it struck with the Houthis last year to end bombing in Yemen, recently holding direct talks with the group in Oman.

Indeed, as the Houthis survived each successive campaign, al-Houthi’s ambitions have grown bigger. He now sees them as a regional force, one that can shape Islam and the Middle East, according to Shuja al-Deen, not just one with an eye on capturing more of Yemen.
“They don’t define themselves as a local group, but as a revolutionary transnational group,” she said. “He is looking at Mecca and Medina more than he is looking at Aden.”

“He rarely gives direct orders, preferring to explain what he wants and bring others with him,” said al-Bukhaiti. When the two first worked together, his instructions were so understated that al-Bukhaiti said he sometimes mistook them for advice.

Ali al-Bukhaiti, a former Houthi official and Mohammed’s brother, remembers al-Houthi in 2011 as shy and attentive, often sitting silently through meetings and listening closely. “Personally, I still love him to this day,” said Ali, who later broke with the Houthis. “But I disagree with his ideas.”

As he urged the international community to take the Houthis seriously that year, Benomar said he set out to bring Yemen’s powerbrokers together for dialogue before it was too late. He wanted everyone with influence in the country to be involved, including the young leader of the Houthis.

Tahrir Square in central Sanaa was filled with young people demanding change and an end to President Ali Abdullah Saleh’s three-decade rule. Saleh’s government was jostling with opponents over the country’s future. Few were paying much attention to the rebel movement from the north.

After coordinating with Mahdi al-Mashat, then in his mid 20s and now president of the Supreme Political Council of the Houthis, Benomar traveled north to Saada. He left his UN security detail behind and passed through a series of Houthi checkpoints to reach the stronghold. Benomar remembers driving through rubble and ruins, entire areas levelled by years of fighting.
But the group al-Houthi runs today was galvanized by that destruction.

The Houthis are routinely described as an Iranian proxy. But al-Houthi’s relationship with Tehran developed gradually, initially through the group’s ties with Hezbollah. The Houthi takeover of Sanaa in 2014 forced Tehran to take the group more seriously. After the Saudi-led coalition started attacking Yemen a year later, the Houthis were driven closer to Iran.

Hezbollah was the model. The Lebanese group had survived wars with a far more powerful military power, Israel, while building military and political power. The Houthis sought to replicate that in Yemen. Iran saw that as an opportunity to widen its Axis of Resistance. The Houthis then increasingly became beneficiaries of Iranian expertise, weapons and training.
“They don’t need to be a proxy if they have the same agenda and the same goals,” Shuja al-Deen said. “Iran doesn’t need to give them orders.”

Ties between the Houthis and Tehran entered a new phase after Israel launched its war on Gaza in 2023 in response to Hamas swarming into the south of the country, massacring 1,200 people and taking another 250 hostage. The Houthis began firing missiles and drones toward Israel and targeting commercial shipping in the Red Sea, saying they were acting in support of Palestinians.

The campaign boosted al-Houthi’s regional and international profile and cemented the Houthis as a force to be reckoned with. The US has kept intact the truce it struck with the Houthis last year to end bombing in Yemen, recently holding direct talks with the group in Oman.

Indeed, as the Houthis survived each successive campaign, al-Houthi’s ambitions have grown bigger. He now sees them as a regional force, one that can shape Islam and the Middle East, according to Shuja al-Deen, not just one with an eye on capturing more of Yemen.
“They don’t define themselves as a local group, but as a revolutionary transnational group,” she said. “He is looking at Mecca and Medina more than he is looking at Aden.”

title: Brazil’s Richest Banker Adds $2.7 Billion on Bolsonaro Rally
paragraphs: Brazilian billionaire Andre Esteves’ fortune soared by a record amount as shares in his bank, Banco BTG Pactual SA, joined the market frenzy triggered by the right’s surprise showing in the country’s general elections.

Esteves’ net worth rose by $2.7 billion on Monday, a 20% jump, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. That was the day’s biggest gain on the index and pushes his net worth to $15.8 billion, making him the third-richest Brazilian.

Brazilian markets were euphoric on Monday after conservative presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro performed better than expected in a first-round vote, finishing first. Brazilians will vote in a second round in less than three weeks, pitting Bolsonaro against current leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Political and financial analysts say Bolsonaro is entering the runoff with much higher chances than his rival.
Esteves, who is BTG’s main partner, is known for maintaining pragmatic political relationships with both the left and the right. A representative for BTG declined to comment.

Around the same time, Esteves also met with US President Donald Trump in a golf club near Washington, DC, where they discussed Brazil’s economy and elections.
BTG was the sole Latin America-based bank involved in the giant initial public offering of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. earlier this year, which made Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire.

title: AMD’s Su to Meet Samsung’s Chip Head as Memory Crunch Persists
paragraphs: Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s chief executive officer plans to meet with the head of Samsung Electronics Co.’s semiconductor business on Wednesday, the latest in-person catchup between two of the AI industry’s key figures.

Lisa Su will meet with Samsung Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun, who leads the pivotal chip division, during her visit to South Korea, a person familiar with the matter said. The person, who asked not to be named discussing private matters, did not elaborate further.
Representatives of Samsung and AMD declined to comment.

The meeting comes as shortages in a broad array of memory products strain the global electronics industry and challenge the expansion of AI infrastructure and services. Memory prices are surging, becoming one of the biggest costs for data-center operators. In March, AMD and Samsung agreed to a supply deal for next-generation high-bandwidth memory as well as advanced memory chips.

The visit marks the AMD CEO’s second trip to Seoul in seven months. South Korea occupies a critical position in the global tech ecosystem as both a major supplier and a consumer of artificial intelligence hardware. The country is orchestrating investments worth $880 billion from companies including Samsung and local peer SK Hynix Inc. into digital infrastructure and data centers for the AI era.

Samsung and SK Hynix supply the HBM required for many of the world’s advanced AI accelerators. At the same time, Korea’s top telecommunications, and manufacturing and internet platform companies are aggressively ramping up investments in AI data centers and next-generation enterprise services.

title: Indonesia VP Stays in Office as Court Quashes Diploma Challenge
paragraphs: Indonesia’s Constitutional Court dismissed a bid to unseat Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka over his educational credentials, keeping former President Joko Widodo’s son in office even as the judges cast doubt on whether he met the requirements to run in 2024.

The court late Tuesday declared inadmissible a petition that sought to remove Gibran, saying the petitioners were not participants in the 2024 presidential election and therefore lacked legal standing to bring the challenge.

The judges did say, however, they found no convincing evidence that Gibran held a foreign diploma or other graduation document showing he had completed education equivalent to an Indonesian high school education — a requirement to run. Even so, they didn’t rule Gibran had failed to meet the requirement and added the court couldn’t disqualify him through an election-results dispute after he’d been inaugurated as vice president.

The ruling keeps Gibran in office but leaves questions about his educational credentials unresolved nearly two years into his term as coalition parties begin maneuvering over who might join President Prabowo Subianto for a possible re-election bid in 2029.

The petitioners, who included a former deputy law minister, an election monitoring group and a political party among others, had asked the court to disqualify Gibran and annul his inauguration as vice president. They also sought to have national lawmakers and regional representatives choose a replacement from candidates proposed by Prabowo within 60 days.
The General Elections Commission, or KPU, didn’t respond to request for comment.

Gibran’s path to the vice presidency was opened by an earlier controversial Constitutional Court ruling. In October 2023, the court created an exception to the minimum age requirement for presidential and vice-presidential candidates that allowed the then 36-year-old to join Prabowo’s ticket.

That ruling drew scrutiny because then-chief justice Anwar Usman, Gibran’s uncle, participated in the case. The court’s ethics council later found Anwar had committed ethical violations, including breaches of impartiality and independence, and removed him as chief justice. The age ruling itself remained binding.
Prabowo and Gibran went on to win 96.2 million votes, or 58.59% of valid ballots, in the February 2024 election.

The latest case centered on a 2019 Education Ministry certificate that assessed Gibran’s overseas education as equivalent to completing an Indonesian vocational high school. The ministry told the court that the assessment considered his combined academic records from Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore and UTS Insearch in Australia.

During the hearings, officials also said Gibran’s 2019 application included academic records from UTS Insearch and that the ministry assessed the continuity of his studies, the curriculum and his learning outcomes. Education officials defended the resulting equivalency certificate as a valid government administrative decision.

The challenge was brought more than two years after the presidential election results were declared. Election officials argued the Constitutional Court had no authority to reopen a dispute over candidate eligibility that long after the election, while the petitioners said key documents underpinning their case only became available later.

The KPU had argued the case shouldn’t be heard as a presidential election-result dispute because it concerned candidate eligibility, which it said should have been handled via the election-process dispute mechanism. KPU also challenged the petitioners’ legal standing, saying presidential election-result cases can ordinarily be brought only by participating candidate tickets, not by election monitors, political parties or individual voters.

title: Waymo Boosts Private Debt Deal to $5 Billion in Push for Growth
paragraphs: Waymo increased the size of its inaugural debt raise to $5 billion, tapping lenders to help fuel the robotaxi company’s growth as it expands globally.
Pacific Investment Management Co., Blackstone Inc. and Sixth Street Partners were among investors who participated in the private loan, according to people familiar with the matter.

The deal priced at 5.25 percentage points over the benchmark rate, the people added, asking not to be identified discussing a private transaction. Waymo had earlier sought to borrow more than $3 billion for its first debt deal, Bloomberg previously reported.
The loan has been allocated and is expected to formally close soon, the people said. Waymo worked with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to arrange the deal.
Representatives for Pimco, Blackstone and Goldman Sachs declined to comment. Representatives for Waymo and Sixth Street did not respond to requests for comment.

Waymo, Alphabet Inc.’s autonomous driving unit, is grappling with rising artificial-intelligence costs as it rapidly builds out its fleet of driverless cars. The company is expanding its services to more US cities, including Las Vegas and Detroit, while pushing into Asia with plans to bring its robotaxis to Japan and Singapore in the coming years. Waymo has set a goal of operating 1 million paid weekly rides this year.

Previously, Waymo relied on the equity markets to help fund its growth. The company raised $16 billion at a $126 billion valuation earlier this year, a funding round that reflected its rapid ascent as a robotaxi pioneer, and recently built a custom chip for its self-driving cars.

title: Apple to Launch Doorbell, Lock, Thermostat Developed With LG
paragraphs: Apple Inc.’s upcoming push into smart home devices will include a doorbell, thermostat and other accessories developed through an unusual partnership with LG Electronics Inc.

The products will be part of an ecosystem of devices that work with Apple’s new smart home hub, as well as an upgraded HomePod mini and fresh TV set-top box, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The new Apple devices are set to be introduced on Oct. 13.

The products developed with South Korea’s LG will also include a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the undertaking is private.
Though the two companies worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand. The South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support.
Apple has used this strategy before: It has discreetly worked with companies like Foxconn Technology Group’s Belkin and Logitech International SA to develop products that sell under other brands.

This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.

Development of the LG accessories has lagged behind Apple’s own devices, and the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months. Spokespeople for Apple and LG declined to comment.

In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organizations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories.

That includes products labeled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor. LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early next year. The filings don’t mention Apple’s involvement.

Many of the devices include support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth networks, as well as Thread and Matter, two smart home protocols embraced by Apple and its rivals in recent years. The door lock also supports UWB, or ultra-wideband capability, a feature that allows for auto-unlocking when users approach their door.

For Apple, the new home ecosystem and devices will mark a formal reboot of HomeKit, a platform it launched in 2014 that has gained little traction compared with offerings from Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google.

Apple aims to use its smart home devices and Siri AI assistant to breathe new life into the category. The company is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported.

For LG, a company better known for TVs and washing machines, the devices will mark its own smart home expansion. The lineup represents its first indoor camera in nearly a decade, as well as its first outdoor camera, thermostat, floodlight camera and doorbell in recent history. The company also is selling its first smart lock outside of South Korea.

This would put Apple and LG in closer competition with Amazon’s Ring and Google’s Nest, which are firmly entrenched in the smart home. Each already offers similar devices that let customers keep tabs on every corner of their house and surrounding property.

Apple and LG have a long history. Once rivals in the smartphone space, Apple and some of LG Electronics’ sister companies are critical partners. LG Display supplies displays for many Apple products, including screens for devices. Apple has also worked with LG Electronics on integrating its services into LG TV sets.
Nearly a decade ago, when Apple temporarily exited the external computer monitor market, it codeveloped monitors with LG to work with the iPhone maker’s laptops.

title: Australians Are Less Vulnerable to Rate Hikes, Deutsche Says
paragraphs: Australian households are proving less vulnerable to interest-rate increases than their heavy debt loads might suggest, Deutsche Bank AG said, noting stronger household balance sheets are helping borrowers withstand tighter monetary policy.

Household assets have continued to grow strongly while debt relative to income has leveled off, macro strategist Lachlan Dynan said in a research note released Wednesday. On a measure that weighs debt against assets, he estimates household leverage has fallen to its lowest since 1997.

“As a result, the cash-flow channel of monetary policy looks to be less potent vs the last decade, while the broader household balance sheet — beyond housing — may also be helping offset any resulting wealth effects from softer house prices,” Dynan said.

Australia has some of the highest household debt in the developed world, and combined with most borrowers being on variable rates, the Reserve Bank’s four hikes this year have flowed straight through to mortgage repayments. This, combined with surging fuel costs and falling property prices, should have pushed household finances toward their limit.
Yet consumer spending has actually strengthened in 2026.

“Fears of rates ‘breaking’ the household sector may be overblown,” Dynan said. “In the context of persistently high core inflation pressures, and energy impacts that may take several more quarters to fully materialize, risks to RBA pricing are back to being skewed to the upside.”

While the RBA delivered a hawkish statement last week when it raised the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6%, Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference was interpreted as more dovish, leaving the outlook for the Nov. 2-3 meeting open and likely dependent on economic data in the interim.
The first of those is likely to be the September employment report out next week.

A handful of economists expect a follow-up move next month to 4.85%, though the median estimate is that the RBA board will keep the key rate unchanged. Money markets see about a 30% chance of a hike in November, a 50-50 chance in December and are almost fully pricing a rate increase at the March 2027 meeting.

title: India’s $110 Billion HDFC Bank Faces Upheaval With Outsider CEO
paragraphs: As HDFC Bank Ltd. prepares for its first outsider chief executive, trepidation is rippling through its senior ranks, with some bracing for the possibility of more shifts in management and power structures inside the $110 billion lender.

Some senior executives had hoped to see long-time Deputy Managing Director Kaizad Bharucha get the top job, people familiar with the matter said. Instead, Anup Bagchi — a external candidate —was handed the role outright.

A lot hinges on Bagchi’s ability to pull off his new job. The stock, held by funds including those from global heavyweights like BlackRock Inc. and Vanguard, has tumbled nearly 30% this year as its chairman quit acrimoniously and its CEO later surprisingly said he wouldn’t seek a new term. The bank is classified as systemically important to the nation’s financial system. And analysts are predicting that some HDFC veterans may leave in the near term.

India is one of the world’s fastest growing economies and, as it gets increasingly interconnected to the rest of the world, behemoths from HDFC to Tata Group are grappling with a variety of complexities as they steer sprawling institutions through changes and new managers.

Bagchi headed ICICI Prudential Life Insurance Co., the life insurer backed by one of HDFC’s biggest rivals, ICICI Bank Ltd. His experience spans from retail banking and digital finance to treasury and insurance. He got the new job partly because he would have wider perspective than a long-time insider in reassessing HDFC’s operations, people familiar with the matter said.

In recent months, internal divisions in HDFC have played out publicly. Earlier this year, HDFC’s previous chairman resigned unexpectedly saying certain practices were not in “congruence with my personal values and ethics.” That sparked a rout in the lender’s shares even though the bank denied any wrongdoing and the regulator came to the bank’s defence. Outgoing CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan later surprised colleagues by deciding not to seek another term.
While Bagchi would be inclined to do things differently, he is unlikely to take steps that would shake the confidence of HDFC employees overnight, a person familiar with the matter said.
Bloomberg spoke to nearly a dozen people familiar with the bank’s operations or with Bagchi’s thinking. They asked not to be identified discussing matters that aren’t public.

HDFC said in a statement that all decisions about senior management are taken by the board or relevant committees after thorough deliberations and discussing broader management changes would be “speculative.”
“The Bank has a history of strong professionalism, and its leadership remains aligned and focused on delivering value for our customers and stakeholders,” the statement said.

One of Bagchi’s top agendas is to bring back investor confidence, people familiar with matter said. He has a challenging job ahead. Shares of HDFC, which has a market value of more than $110 billion, are down nearly 30% for the year.

People familiar with the new CEO say Bagchi, 56, could be well suited to the position because he is strict about details and following regulations. He’s known to be approachable and has a liking for talking to colleagues face-to-face — sometimes even in the office canteen — rather than sticking to the CEO cabin, some of the people said. Colleagues sometimes call him Professor Bagchi for his love of reading and knowledge of a variety of subjects, according to people familiar with the matter.
Former colleagues also describe him as particularly resistant to internal camps, with a habit of moving between teams rather than attaching himself to particular factions.

Macquarie analyst Suresh Ganapathy said his experience across financial-services businesses and proven chief executive leadership could be particularly relevant for a bank navigating a demanding transition.

Yet even if Bagchi takes a measured approach with his changes, some executives could choose to leave. “Any external candidate that gets appointed will have to deal with senior management exits, in our view,” said Ganapathy. “Our channel checks and anecdotal industry feedback suggest that there might be some attrition among long-tenured branch managers.”
Bagchi starts as CEO on Oct. 27. One of the earliest questions will be the role of Bharucha, who had been the leading internal candidate for the top job.

Bharucha’s future will be an early test of how disruptive Bagchi intends to be. A three-decade veteran, he remains a key repository of institutional knowledge. Bharucha staying on could help preserve continuity; losing him could accelerate departures among executives already unsettled by the succession. Bharucha didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The new CEO takes over as recently appointed Chairman Rajiv Kumar pushes for faster post-merger growth, tighter controls and changes in management, Bloomberg News reported in September. Jagdishan resisted parts of that push, helping set the stage for his decision not to seek another term, Bloomberg News reported at the time. HDFC Bank has denied they had such differences and that those were behind his decision.

In the immediate aftermath of the HDFC CEO appointment, two camps emerged internally with one group arguing that the bank would have stabilized more quickly under an insider. Others said Bagchi would be more effective in making changes, with some executives who joined the bank in more recent years hoping he would bring positive changes.
The HDFC statement said it would be misleading to describe internal divisions.
Some in the firm expect Bagchi to double down on a revamp that newly appointed Chairman Kumar began after taking over a few months ago, according to people familiar with the matter.
The push by the new chairman has already started to reshape the bank. The board last week named V.N. Srivatsan, a senior executive at ICICI Bank, as HDFC Bank’s next chief compliance officer.
“While the Bank has well established governance frameworks, we continue to enhance the same, as required,” HDFC said in its statement.

Technology and customer service could also be high on the agenda, people familiar with the matter said. There could also be higher investments in digital systems as well as efforts to address service shortcomings at a bank whose scale has grown sharply since the merger, the people said.

One of Bagchi’s most tangible legacies in an earlier position was ICICIdirect, an online investing platform that helped bring stockbroking and other financial products to a new generation of Indian retail investors who’ve increasingly helped turbo-charge its markets. But the domestic life insurance company he oversaw is a fraction of HDFC’s size.

Meanwhile, he will also inherit heightened regulatory scrutiny. HDFC has faced disputes over sales of Credit Suisse Additional Tier 1 bonds to overseas clients, although it has won all seven cases brought by investors in Bahrain. In September 2025, regulators also barred its Dubai branch from onboarding new customers over alleged compliance lapses. The bank has said it has taken steps to comply with the directives.

Given HDFC Bank’s size and systemic importance, the institution could remain closely watched by regulators as its leadership architecture settles, said Srinath Sridharan, a corporate advisor specializing in succession planning and governance.
“The incoming CEO will need to build a strong working relationship with a board that is itself entering a new phase, while maintaining clarity between oversight and management,” he said.

title: Boston Dynamics Taps Amazon Alexa Executive as New CEO
paragraphs: Boston Dynamics appointed former Amazon.com Inc. executive Rohit Prasad as chief executive officer to lead the Hyundai Motor Co.-controlled company into its next era of innovation and commercialization of its robots.

Boston Dynamics, known for its agile humanoid robots, is currently developing robotic systems for industrial and other real-world environments, an area called physical AI. Hyundai, which acquired majority ownership of Boston Dynamics in 2021, said earlier this year it plans to deploy the unit’s Atlas robot at its plant in Georgia starting in 2028 and build the capacity to produce as many as 30,000 humanoids annually.

Prasad spent 12 years at Amazon helping build and expand smart assistant Alexa. Before joining Amazon, he worked 14 years at Raytheon BBN Technologies overseeing machine-learning research and real-world applications for US government and commercial use, Boston Dynamics said Tuesday in a statement.

Earlier this year, Robert Playter stepped down after six years as Boston Dynamics CEO, only the second leader in that post in the company’s more than 30-year history. Since then, several top executives have left the company, including Chief Technology Officer Aaron Saunders.

At the same time, Hyundai is moving to acquire SoftBank Group Corp.’s remaining stake in Boston Dynamics to secure full ownership of the robotics pioneer. Hyundai has also sealed strategic partnerships with Nvidia Corp. and Google DeepMind to develop Atlas. The robots are expected to begin simple tasks like welding and logistics, before being mobilized for more complex manufacturing processes, including component assembly, by 2030.

title: For Billionaires, AI Wealth Is Different This Time
paragraphs: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.
The boom in AI valuations has created unprecedented wealth for founders, early-stage investors and employees lucky enough to get stock options.

Even among the very richest people in the world, the divergence between the AI haves and the everyone-else-have-nots is stark. Tech billionaires account for all of the $845 billion in wealth gains on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index so far this year, while those who made their fortunes outside technology lost a combined $62 billion.

And being a tech billionaire increasingly means being an AI billionaire. Take the top 10 names on Bloomberg’s wealth index: nine of them attribute their fortunes to firms like SpaceX, Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Nvidia that get at least some of their revenue from AI.

The surging wealth — including Elon Musk’s brief foray as the world’s first trillionaire earlier this year — along with growing fears about AI’s impact on jobs and maybe even human survival have prompted a national backlash. A 5% tax on billionaires will be on the ballot in California in November, and similar measures have been proposed in states including Washington, New York, Illinois and Rhode Island.

Still, there are signs the boom may have peaked, at least for now. The combined net worth of the 500 richest people in the world has fallen 6% since mid-June amid growing doubts about some of the biggest AI names. Among the year’s biggest losers is Larry Ellison, whose fortune has slumped by about $60 billion as investors balk at the massive borrowing needed to fund Oracle’s AI infrastructure build.

Today marks the launch of the redesigned Bloomberg Billionaires Index. You can test out new ways to understand the wealth behind the world’s top 500 richest people by region, industry, age and more.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.
Politics & Policy

The US lead over China in AI has narrowed to a record low of just 3% on benchmark scores, down from 9% in May and 15% earlier in 2026, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. The gap has closed largely due to advances by Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, whose V4.1 Flash model ranked sixth globally on LiveBench after its September release. The shrinking performance gap raises questions about the effectiveness of US export restrictions on chips and the long-term sustainability of American AI supremacy.

SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son, one of AI’s most prominent advocates, struck an unusually cautionary tone at a Kyoto event Sunday, warning that superintelligence in the wrong hands could become “super dangerous.” Son called for international cooperation to manage AI safety risks, saying countries can no longer afford to fight among themselves given the far greater threat posed by powerful AI models.

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who recently quit the company and accused both Anthropic and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives” over AI development risks, will testify Monday at a New York City Council hearing on AI. The hearing will also feature former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner and former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo alongside representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Meta.

South Korea’s Shinhan Bank disclosed that an unauthorized external party accessed customer data belonging to approximately 25,000 people, with cybersecurity experts cited by Yonhap News suggesting that sophisticated AI agents were used to probe for vulnerabilities and breach a service used by loan recruiters. Exposed information included customer names, phone numbers, annual income, and borrowing limits. The bank said it cannot yet quantify the financial impact and is investigating with authorities.

President Donald Trump announced the creation of a “Super Intelligence Force” AI task force, naming Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson as its leaders. Emil Michael and Scott Kupor will also lead the group. The task force will report directly to Trump and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is demanding that Flock Safety delete personal data unconnected to crimes and disclose whether federal agencies have accessed its nationwide AI-powered license-plate database. Schumer said the company has not answered questions about its contracts or how law enforcement is using the collected information. Separately, lawmakers introduced the Ban Flock Act on Oct. 2 to restrict federal use of Flock’s AI cameras, though Schumer stopped short of explicitly endorsing the bill.

NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, has drafted a strategy called “Theory of Victory” outlining how the alliance would defeat a Russian attack on its eastern flank using drones, AI, and other emerging technologies integrated with conventional military power. The document, seen by Bloomberg in unclassified form, is set to be presented in Poland on October 12 amid heightened NATO-Russia tensions. The plan is intended to reassure the public and clarify NATO’s defensive posture, though officials emphasize there are currently no indications Russia is preparing a conventional attack on the alliance.
Banking & Finance

Schneider Electric SE agreed to acquire Boston-based industrial software firm PTC Inc. for approximately $22.6 billion in an all-cash deal — the French conglomerate’s largest acquisition to date — to tap into the AI boom. The deal will add engineering software serving the automotive, aerospace, and medical technology sectors to Schneider’s portfolio.

Wall Street’s AI-driven rally continues to push equity indexes toward record highs, with the Nasdaq 100 hitting a fresh record and up 22% this year, even as long-term Treasury yields reach their highest levels since 2002, with the 30-year bond yield touching 5.69%. Microsoft, Nvidia, and Apple have been the largest contributors to gains in both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 over the past three months. Investors remain cautiously optimistic, with third-quarter earnings per share for the tech sector expected to surge more than 65%, though rising yields are increasingly seen as a mounting risk to the rally.

Nvidia partner Hon Hai Precision Industry reported September-quarter revenue of NT$3.03 trillion ($95.4 billion), a 47% increase that surpassed analyst estimates of NT$2.83 trillion. The strong results, driven by demand for AI infrastructure, add to evidence of sustained global spending on AI alongside a bullish forecast from Micron Technology. Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn, serves as a server assembly partner for Nvidia while also deriving significant revenue from its iPhone manufacturing business with Apple.
Management & Labor

New York City’s AI sector is booming with AI companies leasing more than double the office space in the first half of 2026 than in all of 2025, and startups raising a record $16.7 billion in venture capital last year. But the surge is failing to benefit young job seekers, according to a Partnership for New York City report. Entry-level job postings have fallen sharply in AI-exposed occupations since ChatGPT’s 2022 launch.

Stripe is creating 200 new roles at its Dublin office, including engineering positions, providing a boost to a city disproportionately exposed to AI-driven job cuts. Dublin is particularly vulnerable to AI-related disruption, with more than 6% of its workforce employed in the tech sector — above the EU average — and multinationals including Meta Platforms and TikTok have made significant layoffs there this year.
Bloomberg Opinion

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is deploying a classic populist playbook — targeting wealthy elites and corporate power — but has updated it for the AI era, writes columnist David Drucker. He argues the approach is politically effective but intellectually overblown, framing legitimate policy concerns in alarmist, zero-sum terms.

It did exactly what he wanted, but with an unexpected twist: It found a flaw in the system and canceled the booking of another person on the list.

title: Nearly Half of American Adults Use AI But Few Pay for It
paragraphs: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

The biggest AI companies want investors to see their chatbots and agents as the next great consumer utilities — a daily essential like search or email. But a new report from venture firm Andreessen Horowitz shows that most consumers aren’t willing to pay for AI services, raising questions about the sustainability of giant AI investments ahead of planned IPOs.

Although nearly half of US adults surveyed over the summer use AI chatbots, only 4.5% of consumers in the country had a paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, according to an analysis of YipitData receipts by VC firm Andreessen Horowitz. And that spending is remarkably concentrated: The top 1% of payers account for 19.5% of overall consumer AI spending, shelling out $903 a month on average. The median payer spent just $25 a month.

There also isn’t a ton of overlap between the 50 highest-grossing artificial intelligence apps and those that have the most monthly traffic. Some of the AI players drawing the most spending after ChatGPT and Claude include AI video startup Higgsfield, vibecoding tool maker Replit and AI music startup Suno — all of which rank much lower on Andreessen Horowitz’s monthly web traffic leaderboard.

In other words, the biggest spenders “look less like mainstream consumers and more like prosumers, individuals buying software to build, create, and get work done,” wrote Olivia Moore, an Andreessen Horowitz partner investing in consumer technology.

That creates an awkward question for AI companies investing billions with the promise they can go bigger than selling productivity software to white-collar workers. Moore argues that the business models for these AI products could still evolve beyond subscription plans. The autonomous tools, which can facilitate purchases, may open up the path for companies to collect advertising and transaction fees.

Whether than happens will be critical for AI companies looking to go public and diversify their income streams. After all, they need to prove that they can make money not just from AI power users, but from everyone else.

Banking & Finance

DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan ($12 billion) in its latest round of funding, blowing past its own capital-raising target ahead of a landmark IPO in early 2027, Bloomberg reports exclusively. Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology and WeChat-operator Tencent have committed among the largest amounts in the current financing, which closes soon, people familiar with the matter said.

Nvidia is approaching a $6 trillion market capitalization, making it potentially the first company to reach that milestone, after shares hit a record high following a strong revenue outlook and the announcement of the largest share buyback in history. The stock has gained 28% in 2026, adding $1.2 trillion to its market value and making it the biggest contributor to the S&P 500’s 14% year-to-date gain.

Moonshot AI has closed the final round of private fundraising at a valuation of about $50 billion and is heading toward an IPO in Hong Kong in the first quarter of next year, according to people familiar with the matter. The Chinese AI champion has also begun laying the groundwork to start gauging investor sentiment through early-look meetings starting as early as this month.

OpenAI is in talks with multiple investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi-based MGX, to help anchor a $30 billion round of financing for the ChatGPT maker, according to people familiar with the matter. The UAE funds have discussed putting in as much as $10 billion altogether, one person said. BlackRock is also in discussions to participate in the round alongside that syndicate, the people said.

Bank of America strategists led by Savita Subramanian say the “easy money” from betting on AI capital expenditure beneficiaries over consumer-driven stocks is largely over, as those positions are already heavily priced in. Analysis of long-only active funds shows positioning in “AI disruptee” sectors — including IT services, consumer finance, and software — is near record lows, while industrial stocks are near record highs relative to consumer discretionary. Subramanian noted that white-collar job losses tied to AI disruption pose a continued risk to discretionary spending.

Some potential investors are turning more cautious on the blockbuster IPO of Australian data center firm Firmus Grid, as they worry about existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the company’s debut, according to people familiar with the matter. Firmus priced the IPO at A$11 a share, implying a valuation of about A$43.7 billion ($30.3 billion). The deal — which could raise up to $5.5 billion including the greenshoe option — is shaping up as one of Australia’s largest-ever listings.

The next wave of AI debt financing is taking off in Asia. Companies building hundreds of data centers across the region are also seeking funds to buy the advanced computer chips that will power them. While borrowing to acquire graphics processing units has grown rapidly in the US, the few such loans secured in Asia have mostly involved private credit funds that were willing to take more risk. Now banks are becoming more comfortable with GPU financing.
Economics

Asian economies face significant exposure to a potential AI bust, according to a new report from the Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office, due to their central role in global supply chains and deep integration into AI-related financial markets. The region accounts for two-thirds of growth in global AI-related trade, and a slowdown in demand could shave as much as 1.5 percentage points off economic growth in 2027, which is currently forecast at 4.1%.

Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida described AI as a significant positive demand shock that has put upward pressure on the economy and prices, while also noting that AI could affect the supply side by raising productivity and enhancing capital stock accumulation. Uchida acknowledged uncertainty about the extent to which AI’s economic impact can be captured within traditional monetary policy frameworks.
Technology

Reflection AI, a startup backed by Nvidia and founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers, has unveiled an open-weight AI model called Beam designed for coding and AI agent tasks, claiming it performs comparably to China’s Z.AI flagship model GLM-5.2 at lower cost. The company has held talks to raise $2.5 billion at a $25 billion valuation and has secured billion-dollar computing deals with SpaceX and Nebius Group.

Qualcomm has agreed to license patents underpinning Huawei’s LogicFolding chipmaking technique as part of a multiyear cross-license agreement covering technologies related to 5G devices, AI services, near- and co-packaged optics, and networks. The deal validates Huawei’s semiconductor capabilities and its novel architecture, which focuses on improving data transmission speeds to compensate for China’s lack of access to ASML’s extreme ultraviolet lithography machines. Huawei, which unveiled LogicFolding just months ago, is central to China’s ambitions to lead in AI.

Seagate and Toshiba are locked in a contest for TDK’s magnetic-heads business for hard-disk drives, as the two rivals try to keep pace with demand for AI data-center storage devices. Toshiba initiated talks with TDK in the spring, followed by a higher offer in the summer from Seagate, people familiar with the matter said. The acquisition is expected to be worth as much as several billion dollars.

OpenAI reiterated its apology for its models breaching Australian government websites, pledging to work to prevent similar incidents and to respond faster if they do occur. The activity should not have happened, and the company should have handled its response better, Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon said at a hearing by Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney.
Bloomberg Opinion

India’s technology services sector, a $250 billion export engine supporting 6 million jobs, faces disruption from AI as autonomous agents erode the value of software coding work centered in cities like Bengaluru and Hyderabad. While Indian politicians are attracting Western cloud computing firms with land grants and subsidized energy to build data centers, these investments are expected to generate few new jobs, writes columnist Andy Mukherjee.

Europe has a cohort of companies that are benefiting from the rise of artificial intelligence, and their animal spirits are stirring, columnist Chris Hughes says. Enter Schneider Electric with a surprising and very aggressive $23 billion deal to buy S&P 500 software firm PTC. The deal combines Schneider’s electrical power and industrial software business with PTC’s expertise in computer-aided design, giving Schneider a more comprehensive software offering, he writes.

title: Japan’s Real Wages Rise Again, Aided by Takaichi’s Relief
paragraphs: Japanese workers’ real wages rose for an eighth straight month, the longest streak of gains in almost a decade, as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s inflation-relief measures helped bolster households’ purchasing power.

Real cash earnings — adjusted for inflation excluding rents — climbed 1.5% in August from a year earlier, the labor ministry reported Wednesday, matching the median economist forecast. The ministry said that the increase was underpinned by steady growth in base salaries, which rose 3.8%.

Nominal wages also increased 3.8%, staying above 3% for a seventh month, the longest such run since 1992. A more stable gauge that strips out bonuses, overtime and sampling distortions rose 2.8% for full-time workers.

Takaichi’s utility subsidies helped keep the year-on-year increase in the overall consumer price index at 1.9% in August. The premier touted her efforts during a policy speech Monday to mark the start of a new session of parliament, noting that price relief measures had helped give Japan the lowest inflation rate in the Group of Seven. That, in turn, is helping the nation’s real wages rise at the fastest pace among its peers.

“With nominal wages rising and inflation stabilizing, real wages are managing to stay in positive territory, which should help underpin private consumption,” said Ryosuke Katagi, market economist at Mizuho Securities. “While government subsidies are playing a role in keeping consumer prices in check, I believe the primary factor is the solid growth of nominal wages.”

The government is now aiming to give households further relief by cutting the sales tax on food to 1% from 8% for two years starting in April, a key issue to be debated in the extraordinary Diet session now underway. How the plan takes shape could affect Takaichi’s strategy for managing fiscal policy and determine whether her public support remains firm.
Read: Takaichi Faces Test of Economic Agenda as Japan Parliament Opens

Wage gains have been supported by healthy corporate earnings. Ordinary profits across all industries hit a record in the quarter through June, buoyed by artificial intelligence-related demand and a weaker yen, Finance Ministry data showed last month. Business sentiment has also held up, with the Bank of Japan’s latest Tankan survey showing confidence among large manufacturers at its highest in more than eight years.

“Corporate earnings have been very strong so far this year, with EPS raising nearly 30% from last year on a TOPIX basis,” said Kohei Okazaki, chief market economist at Nomura Securities. “I think we can be fairly optimistic about winter bonuses this year.”
What Bloomberg Economics Says...

“The details suggest the underlying trend is holding firm and support the Bank of Japan’s view that it is gradually securing its 2% inflation target. We expect the central bank to deliver a 25-basis-point hike in December.”
— Taro Kimura, economist
Click here to read full report

Strong profits and improving business confidence provide a favorable backdrop as workers prepare to begin the next round of annual wage negotiations known as “shunto.” Japan’s largest labor union federation typically announces its pay target for the coming fiscal year as early as this month. Workers represented by the group secured increases of more than 5% for a third straight year in this year’s round of talks.

“In the last shunto round, smaller companies followed the lead of larger firms in raising wages,” Okazaki said. “In that sense, it’s hard to imagine wage growth at smaller companies falling far behind or slowing sharply in the upcoming round.”

Sustained wage growth has been a factor paving the way for the BOJ’s interest-rate hikes. Last month, after hiking the benchmark rate for the second time in three months, the central bank signaled the need for further tightening by underscoring the risk of inflation overshooting its 2% target. Authorities cited increasingly proactive wage- and price-setting behavior among companies as one source of upward price pressure.

While most economists expect the BOJ to hold its policy settings steady when the next board meeting concludes on Oct. 30, as of Wednesday morning in Tokyo, overnight index swaps showed markets were pricing in a 76% probability of another rate hike by the end of the year.

Japan’s demographic challenges have been a key factor driving wage momentum. Chronic labor shortages have forced companies to compete for talent by raising pay levels. Some companies unable to pass the higher input costs on to customers have struggled.

Bankruptcies caused by labor shortages rose to a record 240 in the first half of fiscal year 2026, according to a report Tokyo Shoko Research released Monday. More than half were attributed to rising personnel costs, underscoring mounting financial pressure on smaller businesses, the firm said.
It remains unclear whether higher wages will translate into stronger spending. Private consumption remains fragile, with household spending falling for eight straight months through July.

”Headline figures slowed somewhat, but August isn’t really a bonus month, so I don’t think this is likely to alter the BOJ’s view so far — that wage growth has remained solid since the start of the year,” Okazaki said.

title: Musk’s SpaceX in Talks to Borrow $40 Billion to Buy Nvidia Chips
paragraphs: Elon Musk’s SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion of debt to buy chips from Nvidia Corp., people familiar with the matter said, underscoring the insatiable demand among AI developers for more computing power.

Pacific Investment Management Co. is one of the investment managers looking at the deal, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the talks are private. SpaceX’s fundraising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said.

Musk’s AI, satellite and rocket conglomerate is seeking to raise about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips, the Financial Times reported earlier, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. Apollo Global Management Inc. is leading the financing, in a deal that is expected to close in 2027, the newspaper said.

Tech companies and AI model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centers full of chips to power AI systems. The worldwide expansion of computing capacity has sent the cost of everything from land to chips and power-generation equipment soaring, touching off a series of massive financing deals.

Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. SpaceX shares erased gains in postmarket trading following the FT’s report, falling 1.2% in US postmarket trading to $169.79. Nvidia’s stock rose fractionally.

Just last month, Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by the end of the year. It was the most detailed timetable that the trillionaire has given yet for expansion plans for the Memphis-area cluster.

Colossus 2 now has 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s, Musk said in a post on X. A further 220,000 GB300s are due to be operational next week, with another 220,000 expected in November, he said. An additional 220,000 may come online late December “if we get lucky,” he said.
Musk’s xAI has recruited multiple Wall Street firms to test its Grok chatbot, including Apollo and Morgan Stanley.

Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure. The coalition — which also includes Blackstone Inc., BlackRock Inc., Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and KKR & Co. — said at the time that they’d “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers.”

Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signaled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify toward this commitment.
